There isn't a single age when everyone should start taking collagen. In your 20s, your body still produces plenty of collagen, so supplements are usually optional. Starting in your mid-to-late 20s, natural collagen production gradually begins to decline. Many people choose to start collagen supplements in their 30s or 40s when they notice changes in skin elasticity, joint comfort, or hair and nails. In your 50s and beyond, collagen supplementation may be more beneficial because natural production decreases further. If you're healthy and eat a balanced diet with enough protein, you may not need a collagen supplement at all. Foods rich in protein, vitamin C, zinc, and copper help your body make its own collagen. If you're considering collagen, a typical dose is 2.5–10 grams of collagen peptides daily, depending on your goal. Take collagen consistently every day (around 10 g is common). Use sunscreen daily—sun exposure is one of the biggest causes of skin aging. Stay hydrated. Eat plenty of fruits, vegetables, and protein. Get regular exercise and sleep. Results are usually gradual. Many people notice changes in skin texture and hydration after about 2–3 months of regular use. A simple anti-aging routine at 51 that often gives more visible results than collagen alone is: Morning: vitamin C serum + moisturizer + sunscreen.
